question.value: Why is CH3OH emission found at the periphery of starless cores, and how do starless cores grow: are the CH3OH and N2H+ emission offset because turbulence-induced shocks (gas piling onto dense cores in filaments) desorb icy mantles?

referee_caveats_inferred: Only five cores in one cloud; the shock interpretation rests largely on visual inspection of channel maps with no quantified significance of velocity offsets
The simulation places CH3OH only where the velocity jump exceeds 0.4 km/s, so reproducing the CH3OH distribution is partly built into the model assumption
Mass assembly rate depends on X, l, T = 10 K and a sqrt(3) projection factor; no uncertainty is given
Mechanical removal is favoured mainly from a single non-detection of the 20 K line; excitation or abundance differences are not tested
Calibration and spectroscopic constants are not documented, limiting reproducibility; no quantitative model-data comparison (only qualitative)

missing_for_reproduction: Calibration choices and the calibrated measurement sets (pipeline vs. manual, version)

Simulation snapshot, viewing geometry and SPARX/imaging-simulation settings
Statement on data availability and released products
reproducibility.estimated_data_volume_inferred: Five fields of 12-m Band 3 C-2 data; raw MS likely tens of GB, imaged cubes for two 59 MHz SPWs a few GB (guess)
reproducibility.score_reason: Scale 1-10. Observational recipe (project code, tclean settings, line choice) is mostly given but calibration, spectral constants and line-free channels are missing; the MHD/SPARX comparison is qualitative and under-specified; key results are few and loosely quantified.
reproducibility.rediscovery_reason: The paper gives the project code but does not state that the data are public, and the simulation and mass assembly rate recipe lack details; the main conclusion is qualitative with only a few numeric results.
